title: UNFPA: Bangladesh must cut child marriage 20 times faster
excerpt: On the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage, UNFPA said marriage among girls aged 15-19 has risen to 39% and adolescent births to 92 per 1,000.
content:
Bangladesh must speed up its efforts twentyfold to end child marriage by 2030, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) said on Friday (27 November), the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage, The Daily Star reported. The day falls during the 16 Days of Activism against gender-based violence.

In a statement, UNFPA Representative in Bangladesh Catherine Breen Kamkong said the country's progress was not enough to meet the 2030 target. Citing the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025, UNFPA said 47.2% of women aged 20-24 were married before 18 and 13.4% before 15. The rate has fallen by 4.2 percentage points since 2019, less than one point a year.

At the same time, UNFPA said, marriage among girls aged 15-19 has risen to 39% and the adolescent birth rate has increased to 92 per 1,000 girls. Kamkong named poverty, climate shocks and gaps in the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 as reasons girls remain at risk. She said keeping girls in school through higher secondary education cuts the risk of child marriage nearly threefold.

UNFPA called on partners to scale up proven work under the National Action Plan to End Child Marriage, close legal loopholes, give adolescents barrier-free sexual and reproductive health services and regulate marriage registrars (kazis) to stop underage registrations. The UN General Assembly named 27 November as the day in September 2026; this year's theme is "Keeping the Promise: Accelerating Action to End Child Marriage by 2030".

Save the Children, marking the same day in a global statement, said nearly one girl is married every three seconds worldwide and global rates have fallen only from 21.9% to 18.5% since 2014. It cited Bangladesh as a country where rates fell from 62.7% to 47.2% over roughly the same period, crediting sustained investment in social protection, girls' education, community norm change and work against gender-based violence.

Why it matters

The rise in marriage among 15-19-year-olds and in adolescent births suggests recent gains are fragile. Devlens' summary of the MICS 2025 district atlas showed the widest gaps are in specific districts, which is where NGO programmes on girls' schooling, cash support and adolescent health services will matter most.

What to watch

  • Any government move to amend the special provision in the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017 or to tighten kazi registration.
  • Funding for adolescent health services as aid budgets shrink.
  • Events through the 16 Days campaign, which ends on 10 December (see the Events page).
